Chapter 9: Honoring the Past, Shaping the Future—The Fight for Martin Luther King Jr. Day
Sometimes, the fight for justice isn't just about what we do in the present—it's about how we remember. It's about making sure the stories that shaped us aren't forgotten. For Coretta Scott King, this was deeply personal. One of her most heartfelt battles was to create a national holiday for her husband, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.
You might think the idea for Martin Luther King Jr. Day was welcomed right away—but it wasn't. There were political hurdles, arguments about what it would cost, and even folks who just wanted to leave the pain of the past behind. But Coretta? She wouldn't let those things stop her. She knew this holiday was about so much more than honoring just one man. For her, it was a way to remind America that our journey toward justice wasn't finished yet.
Year after year, Coretta kept moving forward. She led marches, met with lawmakers, and inspired crowds in schools, churches, and community centers. Whenever she spoke, her message was clear—the holiday should be more than a break from work. It should be a call to serve others. Sure, there were setbacks—bills that didn't pass, promises that faded—but Coretta never lost hope.
Picture this: one cold winter, while Congress was still debating, Coretta stood on the Capitol steps, surrounded by people who believed in the dream. The wind was biting, but her voice never wavered. She reminded everyone of the sacrifices that had been made, the dreams that still waited, and the hope that refused to die. It was a powerful moment—a reminder that this holiday wasn't just about looking back, but about looking ahead. It was a chance for every generation to ask, "What can we do to keep moving justice forward?"
And when the day finally came—the day the holiday was signed into law—Coretta didn't just celebrate a win. She saw it as a promise fulfilled. But she also understood the real work was just beginning. The next day, people would show up in classrooms, in neighborhoods, and in their own hearts, ready to serve. Coretta kept traveling, kept speaking, urging all of us to honor the day by doing something good—by learning, by helping, by standing up.
Most folks see holidays as a time to rest, but Coretta saw them differently. To her, every holiday was a chance to start fresh—to remember, and then to act. She believed that honoring the past is how we shape what comes next, and that every time we remember, we plant a seed for real change.
